toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: none of the eight admissible publishers address toxicity to pets or humans for Acer palmatum specifically; left null rather than inferred from the Acer genus.

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: sources describe the soil qualitatively as 'slightly acidic' (Clemson, MOBOT), tolerant of 'acidic' to 'slightly alkaline' (UF/IFAS), or 'Acid or Neutral' (RHS), but none give a numeric pH range, so both fields are left null.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, day_f_max/min, night_f_max/min, direct_sun_hours_max, light_fc_min/good: these read as indoor-microclimate fields; no admissible source discusses ambient humidity, indoor temperature comfort ranges, or foot-candle/sun-hour light measurements for this outdoor landscape tree.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: MOBOT says only 'Fertilize in spring before leaves emerge' and RHS (container culture) says 'general purpose granular feed in late spring' -- both name a season, not a specific calendar month, so fertilize_active_months cannot be populated under the month-name rule; no feeding interval or dilution strength is given anywhere.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source frames watering as a checkable schedule (soil-probe depth, days-between-waterings) for this in-ground landscape tree; sources only describe keeping soil evenly moist and watering during the first-year establishment period and dry spells.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source describes a distinct cool/dormancy-rest care regimen beyond noting the tree is winter-deciduous and cold-hardy within its rated zone.

Container/bonsai culture: RHS's growing guide extensively documents growing Japanese maples in outdoor containers (John Innes No. 2 or ericaceous potting mix, root-pruning/repotting every 2-3 years, winter pot protection), and Clemson/NC State note patio and bonsai use -- but this is outdoor container culture, not indoor houseplant use, so is_houseplant is kept false. No schema field distinguishes 'outdoor container' from garden-bed planting, so soil_base is set to garden_bed as the primary, most-supported growing context rather than left null.

water_regime: RHS's container-specific instruction ('keep the compost moist, but not soaking wet, allowing it to begin to dry out between waterings') differs in emphasis from the in-ground guidance (NC State, MOBOT, Clemson all specify evenly/consistently moist soil). This reads as normal container-vs-ground technique variation rather than a genuine disagreement about the species' moisture preference, so keep_moist was kept rather than nulled, but the container nuance is noted here for transparency.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The value 'moderate' does not appear, in substance or in wording, in any of the citations offered for it. NC State's own structured field reads 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage / Moist' (verified verbatim), RHS's structured field reads 'Moisture: Moist but well-drained' (verified verbatim), MOBOT's Culture text says 'well-drained soils... in full sun to part shade' (verified verbatim), and Clemson's Japanese Maple section says soil should be 'well-drained' with drainage good enough that water never stands around the roots (verified verbatim). Every admissible source that addresses drainage at all describes it as good/well-drained, not as a middling or moderate drainage capacity -- so labeling the category 'moderate' asserts a distinction none of the cited quotes actually draw.

records.name_note: No conflict on the accepted binomial. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists "Lagerstroemia chinensis" under "Previously known as," confirming Lagerstroemia indica is the current name and chinensis a historical synonym, and RHS independently flags "Lagerstroemia indica" with "Name Status: Correct." NC State's own common-name list gives "Common Crape Myrtle" as its first/primary listed name, with "Crape Myrtle" also directly listed among the synonyms (alongside Crape Flower, Crepe Myrtle, Indian Crape Myrtle, and Lilac of the South); "Crape Myrtle" was used as this record's common_name.
records.cool_rest_note: In marginal cold climates, plant crape myrtle in a protected location and apply a winter mulch. If the above-ground stems die back in a hard winter, they can be cut back to about 8 inches in early spring; the roots will resprout new stems, typically growing 2-4 feet tall by the end of that growing season.
unknowns: day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: no admissible source gives ambient day/night temperature ranges for this species; only categorical sun-exposure and USDA winter-hardiness-zone data were found, consistent with this being an outdoor landscape tree/shrub rather than a plant grown in a controlled indoor temperature environment.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity requirements for this outdoor tree/shrub.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light values; all sources describe light only as a categorical 'full sun' requirement.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' defines the minimum threshold for its 'Full sun' category, not a maximum for this species, so it was not mapped to this field.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: left null. Clemson and UGA describe outdoor garden-bed watering practice in prose terms ('requires irrigation until it is well-established (approximately two years)'; 'Water crape myrtle plants thoroughly at planting time and once a week...for the first two months after planting') rather than a fixed day-count interval, and established plants are described only as drought-tolerant with supplemental watering recommended 'during dry periods.' None of this maps cleanly to the container-oriented water_regime enum categories (keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist). Per this catalog's own literal-number-derivation standard, a word like 'week' or 'monthly' cannot be converted into a specific day-count without a literal digit in the source text (no source ever writes '7' or '30'), so these fields were left null rather than estimated.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: left null. UGA states fertilizer should be applied 'monthly' to newly planted small plants and gives only a dose amount (1 teaspoon), and for established plants describes only 'one broadcast application... in spring' -- neither is a dilution/strength value (full/half/quarter), and 'monthly' contains no literal digit from which to derive a day-count interval.

fertilize_active_months [3,4,5,6,7,8] (March-August) is scoped specifically to UGA's instruction for newly planted, small (1-gallon) plants during their establishment period: 'To newly planted small plants (1-gallon size), apply 1 teaspoon of fertilizer monthly from March to August along the perimeter of the planting hole.' UGA separately states established, larger plants instead receive 'one broadcast application of fertilizer in spring' with no specific month named -- so this field's value should be read as an establishment-period schedule for young plants, not a universal year-round schedule for mature specimens. Clemson corroborates only in general terms ('Light applications of a complete fertilizer in spring and summer are adequate') without naming specific months.

chill_damage_f -5F comes from Missouri Botanical Garden's statement about growing crape myrtle in the marginal St. Louis climate: 'the above ground branches often die to the ground in winter, particularly when temperatures dip below -5 degrees F.' RHS separately rates the species H3 ('hardy in coastal and relatively mild parts of the UK,' -5 to 1 degrees C), but per this field's own definition (damage-onset, not survival) that H-rating is a general survival-zone classification rather than a stated damage-onset figure, so it was excluded rather than treated as a conflicting value.

cool_rest_note draws on Missouri Botanical Garden's guidance for marginal-hardiness climates (protected siting, winter mulch, and cutting dieback stems back to 8in in early spring, from which the plant resprouts). This is winter-hardiness/dieback-recovery guidance for an outdoor deciduous tree, not a houseplant dormancy note in the sense this field is typically used for, but it is the closest actionable cool-season guidance any admissible source provides for this species.

toxicity_detail: left null. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page tags this species '#non-toxic for cats,' '#non-toxic for horses,' and '#non-toxic for dogs' (supporting toxic_to_pets=false) but gives no further descriptive detail, and the page contains no 'Poisonous to Humans' or symptom section at all to draw from for this species. No other admissible source checked (Clemson, MOBOT, UF/IFAS, RHS, Penn State, UMD, UGA) addresses pet toxicity for this species in either direction, so there is nothing in tension with NC State's tags.

soil_ph_min 5.0 / soil_ph_max 6.5 comes from Clemson's specific statement: 'The plant will tolerate slightly acidic (5.0 to 6.5 pH) clay and other soil textures.' This sits in some tension with NC State's broader categorical tags (Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, AND Alkaline >8.0 all listed as tolerated soil-pH categories) and UF/IFAS's soil-tolerance list, which includes both 'alkaline' and 'acidic.' Missouri Botanical Garden's Problems section, meanwhile, warns 'Foliage may yellow (chlorosis) in alkaline soils,' which cuts the other way and is more consistent with Clemson's narrower, acidic-leaning figure. Since soil_ph is not one of the fields this catalog requires nulling on disagreement (only toxic_to_pets, chill_damage_f, water_regime, and accepted scientific name carry that requirement), Clemson's specific number was used as the only source giving an actual numeric range, with this tension flagged rather than silently resolved.

soil_drainage 'moderate' reflects NC State's mixed Soil Drainage tags (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Occasionally Wet -- spanning more than strict fast-drainage) alongside Clemson's, MOBOT's, and UF/IFAS's consistently stated 'well-drained' language; no source frames drainage narrowly enough to justify 'fast' over this broader tolerance.

is_houseplant is set to false based on this species' outdoor cold-hardiness data (USDA zones 6a-9b per NC State; 7A-9A per UF/IFAS; Zone 6-9 per MOBOT) and RHS's cultivation note that in frost-prone areas it is grown against a wall outdoors or overwintered in an unheated/cool greenhouse rather than kept as a houseplant. Multiple admissible sources do describe outdoor CONTAINER cultivation specifically for dwarf cultivars -- NC State: 'Dwarf varieties may be grown in a container' and tags 'Landscape Location: Container'; UF/IFAS lists 'container or planter' among its landscape Uses -- but none describes sustained INDOOR cultivation, so this container evidence was documented but not read as houseplant status.

No admissible source addresses whether Lagerstroemia indica is toxic to humans, so no human-toxicity claim is made in either direction; NC State's page (the only one carrying the pet-toxicity tags for this species) has no 'Poisonous to Humans' section at all to potentially conflate with the pet-toxicity tags.

Clemson's factsheet (HGIC 1008, titled 'Crape Myrtle') is nominally written for the genus and opens by discussing 'Lagerstroemia species' collectively, but it explicitly identifies Lagerstroemia indica as 'the most common species in the United States' and its cultivar table is overwhelmingly L. indica selections, so it was treated as species-relevant rather than excluded as generic genus-wide boilerplate.

fertilize_active_months — removed on audit: The value [3,4,5,6,7,8] is drawn solely from UGA's instruction 'To newly planted small plants (1-gallon size), apply 1 teaspoon of fertilizer monthly from March to August along the perimeter of the planting hole' (verified verbatim on fieldreport.caes.uga.edu). The SAME source gives established/mature plants a completely different regime: 'one broadcast application of fertilizer in spring' (verified verbatim) -- no monthly cadence, no March-August window. A field named fertilize_active_months will read to a downstream consumer as the general recurring fertilizing window for the species, but the actual value only supports a first-year establishment practice for small container starts; applying it to an established landscape specimen (the far more common state for this plant) would represent six months of monthly feeding where the source instead calls for a single spring application. The unknowns text discloses this scoping, but the field's raw value itself carries no such qualifier and is liable to be consumed at face value.

records.name_note: Admissible sources disagree on which name is currently accepted. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox lists "Benthamidia florida" under "Previously known as" for this species (implying Cornus florida is current), and RHS's own structured "Name Status" field marks "Cornus florida" as "Correct," listing "Benthamidia florida" only under "Synonyms." Penn State Extension's taxonomy article states the reverse: "Cornus florida is now also known as Benthamidia florida, belonging to a new genus that groups together the larger bracted dogwoods," and captions a photo "Flowering dogwood (Benthamidia florida), formerly Cornus florida." Because these admissible sources anchor to opposite current names with no source resolving the conflict, scientific_name_accepted is left null.
records.water_dry_down_target: Water when soil is dry at roughly 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) deep; avoid letting the root zone stay dry for extended periods, especially during the first two years after planting.
records.water_estimate_basis: Based on UMD Extension's establishment-period guidance (check soil moisture weekly for the first two years after planting, water when dry at 4-6 inch depth) plus UF/IFAS's "moderate" drought-tolerance rating and UMD's note that established trees may need irrigation during dry summer months (July-August). No admissible source gives a numeric watering-frequency interval for mature trees.
unknowns: scientific_name_accepted: left null -- NC State Extension and RHS (whose own 'Name Status' field marks Cornus florida 'Correct', listing Benthamidia florida only as a synonym) treat Cornus florida as accepted, while Penn State Extension states the reverse ('Cornus florida is now also known as Benthamidia florida... formerly Cornus florida'). No admissible source resolves this conflict.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: left null -- no admissible source addresses toxicity to pets for this species. Missouri Botanical Garden only hedges on human fruit edibility ('bitter and inedible to humans (some authors say poisonous)'), which doesn't confirm toxicity and never mentions pets.

chill_damage_f: left null -- admissible sources give only USDA hardiness-zone survival data (Zone 5-9/5A-9A, RHS H5), not an actionable cold-damage-onset temperature; expected for a hardy landscape tree, not under-research.

cool_rest_note: left null -- NC State's genus-level Cornus page states 'They... require a chilling period to bloom well,' but that is genus-wide boilerplate ('They' = the Cornus genus) rather than text naming Cornus florida specifically for the chilling claim, so it was not used.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: left null -- admissible sources describe this species only via USDA hardiness zones and sun/shade exposure categories, never in ambient day/night temperature, humidity percentage, or foot-candle terms typical of houseplant records.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: left null -- no admissible source gives a specific fertilizing schedule; UMD Extension explicitly advises fertilizing 'only according to soil test results and not on a regular basis,' recommending annual compost topdressing instead.

water_regime: left null -- none of the fixed regime categories (keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist) cleanly fits UMD's establishment-period practice (check soil moisture at 4-6in deep weekly, water only when dry at that depth) without forcing an awkward fit; that guidance is instead captured in water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, and water_estimate_basis. water_growing_days_est and water_dormant_days_est are also left null since no source gives a numeric watering-frequency interval.

is_houseplant / container or bonsai culture: no admissible source describes growing Cornus florida long-term in a container or as a dwarf/bonsai specimen; UMD's mention of a 'container-grown tree' refers only to nursery stock at planting time, not routine container culture, so is_houseplant is set false rather than left open.

water_check_depth_cm — removed on audit: The value 12.7 is not stated by the UMD quote ('4 to 6 inches deep'); it's an undisclosed midpoint (5in = 12.7cm exactly) that fails the audit's 're-derive the number from the quote' test. Established project precedent for converting a stated depth range takes a literal bound, not a synthesized midpoint -- e.g. Chinese Evergreen (b1): quote 'allow top 1-2 inches to dry' -> water_check_depth_cm 5 (the 2-inch upper bound in cm), not the 1.5in/3.8cm midpoint. 12.7 introduces false precision the source never gave and that this project doesn't otherwise manufacture.

UF/IFAS and UGA both describe a qualitative preference for acid soil with tolerance of a slightly basic/alkaline soil, but neither gives a number.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: this is an in-ground landscape tree, not a container plant. Admissible sources describe planting-time and establishment watering qualitatively (UGA: 'Water thoroughly to settle the soil' at planting, then mulch to conserve moisture; established trees tolerate 'wet/dry fluctuations' per UGA and 'occasionally wet' soil per UF/IFAS, but NC State says the species is 'intolerant to overly wet or swampy soils and prolonged flooding' and MOBOT says it is 'intolerant of soil extremes (dry or wet)'), but none of this maps cleanly onto the container-oriented water_regime categories (keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist) or gives a watering-frequency interval in days.

fertilize_interval_days: UGA gives an establishment fertilizing schedule tied to named calendar months (March, May, July) rather than a fixed day-interval, so no interval_days figure was extracted; see fertilize_active_months and fertilize_strength instead.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: none of the six admissible sources consulted for this species (NC State Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, UF/IFAS EDIS ENH-530/ST371, Clemson HGIC Magnolia factsheet, RHS plant profile, UGA Extension Circular 974) contains a toxicity/poisonous-to-humans or poisonous-to-pets section for Magnolia grandiflora.

is_houseplant / container growing: UGA's 'Container-grown Southern magnolias can be planted successfully any time of year' refers to the nursery-trade form the tree is purchased in (container-grown vs. balled-and-burlapped) before transplanting into the ground, not to long-term container or houseplant culture; no admissible source describes growing this species indoors or permanently in a container (e.g. as a bonsai or patio specimen), so is_houseplant is false with no container-specific carve-out.

outdoor_sun_exposure: UGA's looser phrasing 'Southern magnolia can be grown in sun or shade' was not used to add full_shade to this field, since five more specific admissible sources (NC State, UF/IFAS, MOBOT, Clemson, RHS) all describe the shade-tolerant end specifically as partial shade, not full shade.

soil_base: mapped to garden_bed based on UGA's planting instructions ('plant it in an ornamental bed,' backfill with 'native soil') and MOBOT's 'well-drained loams' culture description; no admissible source frames this species as container-grown long-term, consistent with is_houseplant false.

records.name_note: All three admissible sources treat Pachira aquatica as the current, correct name with no conflict. RHS's own "Name Status" field reads "Correct." NC State lists three superseded synonyms ("Previously known as: Bombax aquaticum, Bombax glabrum, Bombax macrocarpum"), confirming Pachira aquatica as the name that replaced them, not the reverse. Missouri Botanical Garden also uses Pachira aquatica as its primary heading with no conflicting synonym note.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State documents this species' toxicity as seeds-only (cyclopropenoid fatty acids; mild to moderate GI upset in cats -- vomiting, diarrhea, drooling) but states plainly that "houseplants never produce seeds," so the toxic part essentially never occurs on a typical potted specimen. toxic_to_pets is left null rather than an unqualified true, since that would overstate the practical risk for the near-universal houseplant case this record otherwise describes.
unknowns:
toxicity_detail: left null despite toxic_to_pets=true because the only detailed poisoning information on the NC State page is structurally nested under a human-specific header, not a pets-specific one. Direct HTML inspection confirms two separate blocks: (1) a 'Problems:'
containing only the single tag 'Problem for Cats' (used to support toxic_to_pets), and (2) a wholly separate
    block headed by Poisonous to Humans: containing Poison Severity (Low), Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle, and Poison Part. The Poison Symptoms text does name cats ('mild to moderate gastrointestinal distress for cats--vomiting, diarrhea, and drooling') alongside the human carcinogenicity concern, but because that entire detail block sits under a header naming humans specifically, and the toxic principle/severity framing (cyclopropenoid fatty acids, carcinogenicity) is a human-cancer-risk framing rather than a documented pet mechanism, this content was not folded into the pets-target toxicity_detail field per the instruction to check for exactly this kind of human-header nesting before use.

toxic_to_pets is supported by exactly one admissible source (NC State's standalone 'Problem for Cats' tag); Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS's Pachira aquatica pages were both checked directly and neither mentions toxicity, pet safety, or poison information at all for this species -- their silence is an absence of coverage, not disagreement, so toxic_to_pets was not nulled.

humidity_need: NC State states the plant 'thrives in a humid environment with temperatures between 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit' and separately that 'Yellow leaves can occur if the humidity is too low.' This is suggestive but never uses a categorical label (low/average/high) or a percentage, so mapping it to a specific enum value would be an inference beyond what the quote literally supports; left null.
humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives a percentage for this species.

night_f_min/night_f_max: NC State's only temperature statement ('thrives in a humid environment with temperatures between 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit') is a single ambient range with no day/night split, so it was mapped to day_f_min/day_f_max only (following this catalog's established precedent for identical unsplit-range phrasing, e.g. Zebra Plant and Monstera), leaving night fields null since no separate nighttime figure exists.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no admissible source gives an indoor footcandle figure; only NC State's categorical Light field ('Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)') and RHS's Position field ('Full shade, Partial shade') were found, neither of which is a footcandle measurement.

outdoor_sun_exposure full_sun: sourced from Missouri Botanical Garden's own structured 'Sun: Full sun to part shade' tag, which is unconditional in that specific field (unlike a prior case in this catalog where a full-sun claim carried an explicit 'only if' moisture caveat that would have been dropped by including it plainly -- no such caveat is attached to this tag). However, NC State's species-specific structured Light field lists only 'Partial Shade' (no Full Sun option at all) and its prose explicitly warns 'Leaf scorch can occur from exposure to direct sunlight,' specifically in the context of container/houseplant growing. Both signals are preserved: full_sun is included on Missouri Botanical Garden's authority for outdoor/landscape cultivation (its native Zone 10-12 range), but a grower moving a houseplant specimen outdoors or into direct window sun should weigh NC State's scorch caution, which this record cannot fully reconcile into a single flag.

soil_drainage 'moderate' is anchored to NC State's structured tag combination 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist' (for container/houseplant growing, this catalog's primary framing) and corroborated by RHS's 'Moist but well-drained.' This sits in tension with Missouri Botanical Garden's outdoor-landscape framing of this species as a wetland native tolerating 'medium to wet' soil and even standing water for part of the year ('Water: Medium to wet'; 'Tolerate: Wet Soil'; 'Plants grow well in areas that are flooded for part of the year'). NC State's container-specific caution -- 'Standing water is not tolerated and can cause root rot' -- directly contradicts wet/flooded conditions for a potted specimen, so the wetter landscape characterization was not used to loosen soil_drainage; 'moderate' reflects the houseplant-relevant guidance only.

soil_ph_min: NC State lists this species only under the 'Acid (<6.0)' category tag with no defined numeric lower bound, so only soil_ph_max (8.0, from the paired 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' tag) was set, following this catalog's established precedent for the same unbounded-tag pattern (e.g. Sago Palm). RHS's own pH field ('Acid or Alkaline or Neutral') is even broader/unbounded and was not used to override or extend NC State's numeric tag.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: no fertilizing schedule was found on any of the three admissible pages actually fetched for this species (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS's core 'How to Grow' section). Note: a raw fetch of the RHS page transiently surfaced fertilizer text ('Apply a balanced fertiliser every two weeks during the growing season...') and, on a separate fetch, unrelated cultivation text for a different species entirely, plus a stray 'Araucaria heterophylla | Norfolk Island pine' heading -- these did not appear in the RHS page's stable, verified 'How to Grow' block (Cultivation/Propagation/Pruning/Pests/Diseases, confirmed present at a fixed HTML location on every fetch) and are attributed to an unstable, rotating related-plant widget elsewhere on the page. That content was excluded entirely as unreliable rather than used for any field.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a numeric watering interval, moisture-check depth, or dormancy-duration estimate; only qualitative moisture guidance ('needs consistent moisture,' 'moderate but even moisture,' avoid letting soil fully dry or sit in standing water) was found, which supported the categorical water_regime value but not these numeric estimate fields.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source frames any part of this species' care as a deliberate temperature-based rest/dormancy period.

day_f_min/day_f_max chill_damage_f: NC State's instruction to bring the tree 'indoors before temperatures drop to 45 degrees Fahrenheit' was used as chill_damage_f (an actionable pre-damage threshold) rather than as a night_f_min, since the source frames it as a general cold-weather protective action, not a nightly target range; NC State's separate USDA zone 10-12 hardiness rating and RHS's H1B hardiness rating (10-15C survivability threshold) were treated as broader survival-zone classifications and not used to override or duplicate this more specific, actionable °F figure.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The full_sun entry is a genuine, unresolved disagreement on a harm-capable field (leaf scorch), not a case where one clean citation is corroborated elsewhere against a merely defective outlier. Verified via direct fetch: NC State's structured Light field lists ONLY 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' -- no full-sun option exists in that tag at all -- and its prose states plainly 'The money tree prefers indirect sunlight or a mix of sun and shade. Leaf scorch can occur from exposure to direct sunlight,' a general statement, not one scoped only to containers as the record's unknowns text claims. RHS's own structured Position field is 'Full shade, Partial shade' (again, no full-sun option), and its Cultivation instruction says grow 'in bright light or partial shade.' That is two of the three admissible sources -- including an explicit damage warning -- against full_sun; only Missouri Botanical Garden's landscape-context 'Sun: Full sun to part shade' supports it. The record's own unknowns section admits it 'cannot fully reconcile into a single flag,' which is itself the signal that this value should have been left out of the structured array rather than asserted alongside an unrelated caveat buried in unknowns.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: restored toxicity_detail (with a new citation for the previously-uncited poison-detail quote) rather than leaving the nuance out entirely -- the audit's finding that flat toxic_to_pets=true overstates risk for a houseplant that never produces seeds is correct and worth keeping visible, not just discarding.

records.name_note: The given name Araucaria heterophylla is the currently accepted binomial (RHS lists "Name Status: Correct"). NC State lists "Araucaria excelsa" as a former name, and RHS separately lists "Araucaria excelsa misapplied" as a synonym -- both agree the plant is not currently correctly called by that older name, and no admissible source anchors "accepted" to a different binomial, so there is no genuine conflict to null over. Despite the common name and its superficial resemblance to a pine (needle-like juvenile foliage), Missouri Botanical Garden confirms this species "is not part of the pine genus" -- it belongs to family Araucariaceae, not Pinaceae, and is unrelated to Pinus species (the same naming-trap pattern as Sago Palm/Ponytail Palm/Lucky Bamboo elsewhere in this catalog).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags this species "#non-toxic for cats," "#non-toxic for horses," and "#non-toxic for dogs," and the page carries no "Poisonous to Humans" or other poison-severity section for it. This is an explicit non-toxicity statement, not silence. As a sibling-page check: NC State's page for Araucaria araucana (the same genus) carries no such toxicity tags at all, indicating these tags were applied specifically to A. heterophylla rather than copied as genus-wide boilerplate. No other admissible source (MOBOT, RHS, UF/IFAS, Clemson) addresses toxicity for this species one way or the other, so this rests on NC State alone with no cross-source conflict.
records.cool_rest_note: Winter is a reduced-care rest period, not full dormancy: RHS instructs keeping the compost just moist (vs. watering freely in the March-September growing season) and withholding fertilizer entirely during winter months. NC State's indoor-care note similarly says to water sparingly (and mist, in heated rooms) over winter. No source gives a specific temperature target for this winter rest -- the 55-65F figure both NC State and MOBOT give for indoor rooms is presented as a general year-round room preference, not a winter-specific number, so it was not used here.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: NC State and MOBOT both give a single indoor room-temperature preference ("bright, cool room, 55-65 degrees F") without distinguishing day from night, so left null rather than splitting one unlabeled range across four fields.

chill_damage_f: only survival/hardiness-zone data exists, not a damage-onset number. NC State lists USDA zones 9a-11b ("May survive in Zone 9 if provided a warm microclimate" per MOBOT's culture notes); UF/IFAS ST083 lists zones 10A-11; RHS rates it H2, "tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5C)" -- a survival floor, not an actionable damage-onset figure. Per the field's own definition this is expected to be null for a source base that only documents survival zones, not under-research.

humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives a percentage figure; only the qualitative "resistant to... dry indoor atmosphere" / "adapts to the warm, dry atmosphere" language from NC State was found, which was used for humidity_need instead.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good: Clemson HGIC's indoor-plants light-requirements factsheet lists Araucaria heterophylla by name under its "High Light (150 to 1000 ft-c)" category, but the category's own definition ("minimum 150 to 1000 ft-c, 500 to 1000 preferred") spans a wide range shared across many different plants (from succulents to trees) without pinning an individual figure to this species -- unlike the Low/Medium categories on the same page, whose minimum and preferred ranges don't overlap, High's minimum range (150-1000) and preferred range (500-1000) share the same top-end value, so no single defensible min/good pair could be extracted the way it could for e.g. a Medium-light species without effectively guessing where in that span this species sits. Left null rather than assert unwarranted precision.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)" category label states a floor for qualifying as full sun, not a ceiling on hours, and this species is not listed under NC State's Partial Shade category (the only category on that page paired with an hours ceiling, e.g. '2-6 hours'), so no hours-max figure applies.

fertilize_strength: NC State/MOBOT describe 'dilute liquid fertilizer' and RHS a 'balanced fertiliser' -- neither gives a specific dilution ratio (e.g., half or quarter strength) that would map to the fixed enum, so left null rather than guessing a fraction from the word 'dilute' alone.

normalizations: 2026-08-22: sixth batch of the "blind spots" pass. Introduces this catalog's first large landscape trees -- every prior species has been a houseplant, shrub, perennial, or vine. Confirmed by grep that Japanese Maple, Crape Myrtle, Flowering Dogwood, and Southern Magnolia (four of the most commonly planted ornamental trees in US gardens) had zero coverage, alongside four popular houseplants (Ponytail Palm, Money Tree, Norfolk Island Pine, Maidenhair Fern). Two more naming traps in the same vein already documented elsewhere in this catalog (Sago Palm isn't a palm, Lucky Bamboo isn't bamboo, Mini Monstera isn't a Monstera): Ponytail Palm is a succulent-adjacent Asparagaceae, not a true palm, and Norfolk Island Pine is an Araucariaceae, not a true pine.

Two landing-time schema-correctness fixes, both the same defect class as b23's Ceropegia woodii bug: Flowering Dogwood's scientific_name_accepted was written as an empty string instead of JSON null. Its own unknowns text and name_note both already say 'left null' -- a genuine, real naming split (NC State/RHS treat Cornus florida as current; Penn State Extension treats Benthamidia florida as current, with neither side resolving the other) -- so the fix is purely mechanical, matching what the record already intended.

The audit caught a genuinely important, subtle safety nuance on Money Tree: NC State's own toxicity text states the toxic part is seeds-only, in the same sentence as "Houseplants never produce seeds" -- meaning a flat toxic_to_pets=true overstates the practical risk for the near-universal potted-specimen case this record otherwise describes throughout (is_houseplant=true, container-mix soil, indoor overwintering). Rather than just losing this nuance when the boolean was correctly nulled, added the missing citation and restored it as a toxicity_detail explaining the seeds-only/rarely-applicable caveat, so a reader still learns the real, conditional fact instead of nothing at all.

A precise, well-cited catch on Flowering Dogwood: a watering check-depth was recorded as 12.7cm, silently converting UMD's stated "4 to 6 inches deep" range into an undisclosed 5-inch midpoint rather than taking a literal bound the way this catalog has consistently done elsewhere (e.g. Chinese Evergreen in b1, "1-2 inches" -> the 2-inch upper bound) -- correctly nulled as false precision the source never stated.
